claims.title: Theorem~L: Lean-certified statement, v1.4
claims.statement: [Theorem~L: Lean-certified statement, v1.4] Let \(p\) and \(q\) be distinct primes, \(n=p^2q\) and \(N=n+12\), and suppose \(\ph(N)=\ph(n)+12\) and \(\sig(N)=\sig(n)+12\). Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[\textup{(i)}] \(N\) is not prime, and \(N\) is not a product of two distinct primes; \item[\textup{(ii)}] \(N\) is not a product of three distinct primes; \item[\textup{(iii)}] \(N\) is not of the form \(r^2st\) with pairwise distinct primes \(r,s,t\ge 5\); \item[\textup{(iv)}] if \(N=r^3s\) with distinct primes \(r,s\ge 5\), then \(p<r\), \(r^2\) divides \(p^3-p^2-12\), and \(p>10^4\); \item[\textup{(v)}] \(n>10^4\). \end{enumerate}

Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[\textup{(i)}] \(N\) is not prime, and \(N\) is not a product of two distinct primes; \item[\textup{(ii)}] \(N\) is not a product of three distinct primes; \item[\textup{(iii)}] \(N\) is not of the form \(r^2st\) with pairwise distinct primes \(r,s,t\ge 5\); \item[\textup{(iv)}] \(N\) is not of the form \(r^3s\) with distinct primes \(r,s\); \item[\textup{(v)}] \(n>10^4\); \item[\textup{(vi)}] \(N\) is not of the form \(r^k\) with \(r\) prime and \(k\ge 1\), and \(N\) is not of the form \(r^as\) with distinct primes \(r,s\) and \(a\ge 2\); \item[\textup{(vii)}] if \(\omega(N)\ge 4\), then \(q\ge 3p^2\) and every prime \(r\) dividing \(N\) satisfies \(r>p\). \end{enumerate}

claims.title: Values of \(\ph\) and \(\sig\)
claims.statement: [Values of \(\ph\) and \(\sig\)] For distinct primes \(p,q\), pairwise distinct primes \(r,s,t\), and distinct primes \(r,s\) respectively, \begin{align*} \ph(p^2q)&=p(p-1)(q-1), & \sig(p^2q)&=(p^2+p+1)(q+1);\\ \ph(r^2st)&=r(r-1)(s-1)(t-1), & \sig(r^2st)&=(r^2+r+1)(s+1)(t+1);\\ \ph(r^3s)&=r^2(r-1)(s-1), & \sig(r^3s)&=(r^3+r^2+r+1)(s+1). \end{align*} In Lean these are three lemmas.

claims.title: final sentence of Theorem~\ref{thm:E}
claims.statement: [final sentence of Theorem~\ref{thm:E}] Assume~\eqref{eq:jumps} and that \(r^2\mid N\) for some prime \(r\). claims.title: Rigidity equations
claims.statement: [Rigidity equations] Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:closed}. \begin{enumerate} \item[\textup{(a)}] If \(N=rst\) with distinct primes \(r,s,t\ge 5\) and \(\rho\) denotes any one of them, then \begin{equation} q=\rho+\frac{C(\rho)}{D(p,\rho)},\qquad C(\rho)=(\rho-3)(\rho^2+3\rho+8),\qquad D(p,\rho)=2p^2-2p\rho+\rho^2-\rho. \end{equation} In particular \(D(p,\rho)\) divides the \(p\)-free integer \(C(\rho)\). For each prime \(\rho\) there are only finitely many candidate values of \(p\). \item[\textup{(b)}] If \(N=r^3s\) with distinct primes \(r,s\ge 5\), then \(r^2\) divides \(p+q-1\). Writing \(p+q-1=r^2m\) with an integer \(m\ge 1\), one has \(s=pm-r+1\), \(q=r^2m-p+1\), and \begin{equation} pmr^2(r-p)=r^3(r-1)-p^2(p-1)+12. \end{equation} A necessary condition that \(m\) be a positive integer is \begin{equation} p\mid\bigl(r^4-r^3+12\bigr),\qquad r\mid\bigl(p^3-p^2-12\bigr). \end{equation} \item[\textup{(c)}] If \(N=r^2st\) with distinct primes \(r,s,t\ge 5\), write \(\sigma=s+t\) and \(\pi=st\). Then \begin{align} \sigma&=\frac{-(p^3-p^2r-p^2+2pr^3+pr^2-2pr+r^3-r^2-12)}{r\bigl(pr+2p-r^2+r\bigr)},\\ \pi&=\frac{2p^4r+p^4-2p^3r^2-p^3+2p^2r^4-p^2r^2-p^2r-24pr-12p+12r^2-12r}{r(p-r)\bigl(pr+2p-r^2+r\bigr)},\\ q&=\frac{2p^2r^2+p^2r-2pr^3-pr+2r^5-r^3-r^2-12r-24}{(p-r)\bigl(pr+2p-r^2+r\bigr)}. \end{align} In particular a solution is determined by the pair \((p,r)\) alone. The offset families \(r=p\pm 2\) yield \(\sigma<0\) and are empty. (v1.4: the shape \(r^2st\) does not occur at all, by Theorem~\ref{thm:L}(iii); part~(c) is kept as the v1.3 record.) \end{enumerate}

claims.title: Four-prime rigidity
claims.statement: [Four-prime rigidity] Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:closed} and suppose \(N\) is squarefree with four distinct prime factors. Write \(N=rstu\). Then: \begin{enumerate} \item \(\TT(N)=2(e_2+1)\), so \[ e_2=rs+rt+ru+st+su+tu=p+\frac{q-1}{2}. \] AM--GM gives \(e_2\ge 6\sqrt{N}\). Consequently there is no solution with \(q=O(p)\). Comparable-factor quadruples are compatible with this bound only if \(q\asymp 144p^2\). \item For any two of the prime factors, say \(r\) and \(s\), write \(\sigma=t+u\) and \(\pi=tu\). Then \[ \sigma=\frac{N_{\sigma}(p,r,s)}{D_{\sigma}(p,r,s)}, \] where \begin{align*} N_{\sigma}&=-(2p^4-2p^3(r+s)+2p^2rs(r+s)+p^2(rs-r-s+1)\\ &\qquad-2prs(rs)-24p-rs(rs-r-s)+12(r+s-1)),\\ D_{\sigma}&=2p^2(r^2+rs+s^2-1)-2prs(r+s)+rs(rs-r-s+1). \end{align*} The complementary product \(\pi\) is likewise rational in \(p,r,s\). In particular each pair \(\{r,s\}\) determines a curve in \(p\). \item If \(2p^2>rs\), the inequality \(e_2\ge \pi=N/(rs)\) forces the explicit bound \[ q\le\frac{rs(2p-1)-24}{2p^2-rs}. \] \item \(35\nmid N\). Indeed, if \(\{5,7\}\subset\{r,s,t,u\}\) then \(rs=35<2p^2\) for every prime \(p\ge 5\), and the bound of (3) gives \(q<5\) except at \(p=5\) and \(p=7\), both forbidden because \(p\nmid N\). \end{enumerate}
